name: Southeast Gully

waypoints.name: PCT North / Snoqualmie Pass North Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 to Exit 52 (Snoqualmie Pass West) and turn left under the freeway onto Alpental Road. In about 0.1 mile take the first right, signed for the parking pass, and in another 0.1 mile keep right for the main Pacific Crest Trail North lot. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.

approach: Start from the Pacific Crest Trail North (Snoqualmie Pass North) trailhead at about 47.4284, -121.4155, just off I-90 exit 52. Follow the old Commonwealth Basin trail north for approximately 1.4 miles, until Guye Peak lies directly west or northwest of you. From there head straight upslope - the gully initiates directly above. The approach is on maintained trail or, in winter, on whatever bootpack exists, and is short by Cascade standards; the difficulty is judging the snow on the slope between the trail and the base of the gully, which is itself avalanche terrain on a loaded day.

approach_variants.name: Old Commonwealth Basin trail to a bearing of 290 degrees, then straight up
approach_variants.notes:
Start from the Pacific Crest Trail North / Snoqualmie Pass North trailhead at about 47.4284, -121.4155, just off I-90 exit 52. Follow the old Commonwealth Basin trail north for roughly 1.4 miles, or the bootpack that stands in for it in winter.

When Guye lies directly west or northwest of you, leave the trail and go straight up the slope. The walking is short by Cascade standards; the difficulty is judging the snow on the slope between the trail and the gully, which is itself avalanche terrain on a loaded day.

About 2.25 km and 2,100 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: Winter and early spring, roughly January to April, when the gully is filled and consolidated. The ideal is a cold night followed by a clear cold morning; by late spring the sunlit half turns to slush and the route becomes a wet-avalanche problem
hazards: Avalanche is the primary objective hazard — a confined gully below a summit ridge on a slope that loads readily
Sustained steep snow to about 70 degrees with essentially no protection; a fall in the upper section is unarrestable
Cornice formation at the exit onto the ridge between the true and false summits
Rapid sun-warming of the exposed half producing wet slides and rollerballs later in the day
Both descents — Cave Ridge west, Commonwealth east — cross avalanche terrain of their own, and the west bootpath is easily lost under snow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Take a bearing, because this one can be done blind. Walk the old Commonwealth Basin trail about 1.4 miles until the summit of Guye bears roughly 290 degrees — west-northwest — from you, then turn and go straight uphill. A published fix for the start of the route is about 47.4411, -121.4026. In cloud that pair of numbers settles it and nothing on the ground has to be seen.

What the ground should do, in order, once you commit: the route starts by going 45 degrees straight up. Only then does the gully proper develop, turning northwest for about 40 m and steepening as it turns. After that it runs directly at the summit, which stays visible for much of the climb on a clear day. If the ground you are on stays uniformly angled and never turns northwest, you are on the open slope beside the gully rather than in it.

The angle is the other test: this is the steepest of Guye's gully lines. About 45 degrees for the first few hundred feet, then progressively steeper, reaching roughly 70 degrees near the top. A gully that stays moderate all the way is one of the peak's other lines.

Where it puts you: it finishes at the ridge between the true and false summits — not on a summit. If your line tops out on a summit block, it is not this one.

And a conditions test that is part of the finding here: roughly half the gully sits in shade and half in sun, which is what gives it solid snow under the surface. It also means the two halves can be in quite different condition on a warm day.
